profile.address: 17, Cable Drive, Bayview, Tuckerton, Ocean County, New Jersey, 08087
profile.reading:
This cable landing station in Tuckerton, New Jersey served TAT-14, a transatlantic fiber optic telecommunications cable that connected North America to Western Europe for nearly two decades. TAT-14 ran in a ring topology spanning 15,428 kilometers and landed at seven points: Manasquan and Tuckerton in New Jersey on the American side, and Widemouth Bay in the United Kingdom, Saint Valery en Caux in France, Katwijk in the Netherlands, Norden in Germany, and Blaabjerg in Denmark on the European side. The ring design meant traffic could be automatically rerouted around a cable break at any single point without a total loss of service, a significant reliability advantage over earlier point to point transatlantic cable systems.

The cable entered service on March 21, 2001, initially designed for 1.87 terabits per second of capacity and later upgraded using wavelength division multiplexing technology to a total system capacity of 9.38 terabits per second. It was built and owned by a consortium of 11 telecommunications carriers, recorded in cable industry references as AT&T, BT, C&W, Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, KPN, MCII, PGE, Sprint, Swisscom, and Telia, reflecting the international, consortium based ownership model common to major transatlantic cable systems of that era, in which multiple national carriers jointly financed construction and shared capacity rather than any single company owning the system outright.

TAT-14 was decommissioned on December 15, 2020, after nearly 20 years of service, becoming the first transatlantic cable system retired since the Gemini cable in 2003, as newer, higher capacity fiber systems built in the years since made its older technology increasingly redundant. The Tuckerton site has a longer history as a cable landing location, having previously hosted infrastructure for earlier, also since retired transatlantic systems including TAT-3, TAT-4, and TAT-8, cable generations tracing back to the Cold War era of transatlantic telecommunications. Tuckerton's role as a cable landing point continues today, separate from TAT-14, through the currently active GlobeNet cable system, which lands nearby. AT&T's historical role at this location was as one of the 11 original consortium members and carriers on TAT-14 rather than as the sole owner or operator of the site, consistent with how transatlantic cable landing stations were typically structured and staffed during that cable's operating life.

profile.address: 33 Thomas Street, Tribeca, New York, NY
profile.reading: Per the Wikipedia article on 33 Thomas Street, this New York City building (also known as the AT&T Long Lines Building) sits on the east side of Church Street between Thomas and Worth Streets in Tribeca, Lower Manhattan. It is 550 feet tall with 29 floors and was built from 1969 to 1974 as a telephone exchange facility housing long-distance switching equipment, designed for self-sufficiency with independent gas and water supplies and protection from nuclear fallout. The article states it currently operates telephone switching equipment and secure data centers, and reports that journalists have documented it as housing an NSA surveillance hub, a claim this session did not independently verify. This is a Wikipedia article, not an AT&T publication; no square footage or power capacity in MW is stated. Also known as the AT&T Long Lines Building, this tower was completed in 1974 after construction began in 1969, built for AT&T's long-distance telephone switching operations during the era before the 1984 Bell System breakup, when AT&T operated as a single vertically integrated national telephone monopoly. Its windowless, fortress-like design reflects Cold War-era resilience engineering: independent gas and water supplies, filtered air systems, and construction intended to withstand nuclear fallout, a design philosophy shared with a small number of other AT&T Long Lines switching buildings built in major US cities during the same period. The building remains active today housing telephone switching equipment and secure data center space, per the Wikipedia article on the building, though this registry does not independently confirm the specific tenants or the extent of AT&T's continued operational role at the address today versus that of other carriers or government entities reported by journalists to have equipment there. No square footage or power capacity figure specific to this building's current data center use was located in sourcing reachable this session.

profile.legal_history: Originally incorporated March 3, 1885 as American Telephone and Telegraph Company. Reorganized multiple times through the Bell System and its 1984 breakup. In 2005, SBC Communications acquired AT&T Corp for $16 billion and renamed itself AT&T Inc., adopting the historic name and stock ticker T. AT&T Corp continued to exist as a legal subsidiary until it was merged into AT&T Enterprises, Inc. (converted to an LLC) on May 1, 2024, ending its existence as a separate corporate entity.
profile.research_note: This registry treats the 'American Telephone & Telegraph' operator record as the historical legal name of this same company (see duplicate_of on that row); do not treat them as unrelated entities.

reading.body:
AT&T operates three documented facilities in the United States with unknown power capacity, all located in legacy telecommunications infrastructure rather than purpose-built data centers.

The three sites span different facility types and geographies. The New York facility at 33 Thomas Street is a 550-foot, 29-floor building completed in 1974 as a telephone exchange and long distance switching hub, now housing telephone switching equipment and secure data centers. The Tuckerton, New Jersey site is a cable landing station with historical connections to transatlantic telephone cables, though its current operational status remains unconfirmed. The Palmdale, California facility appears to be a traditional telephone central office that lacks independent corroboration in wholesale data center directories.

This portfolio reflects AT&T's distinct position as an incumbent telecom operator with decades of legacy real estate alongside newer data center operations. The absence of megawatt figures for all three facilities indicates they either do not publicly disclose power consumption or operate at scales that differ from purpose-built hyperscale data centers. The data does not clarify which of these facilities currently support AI workloads, which serve only legacy telecom switching, or what fraction of AT&T's total data center footprint these three sites represent. AT&T's data center strategy and power consumption remain largely undocumented in this registry.
